title: Asymmetric Wedge Shawl
subtitle: Garter-effect double crochet rows with a single edge increase for a wedge silhouette
excerpt: A wedge-shaped shawl worked in rows of double crochet with one increase at a single edge on every row. The asymmetric shape and garter-effect ridging come entirely from the dc stitch worked into the back loop only, without any complex shaping.
sourceNotes: Original pattern synthesised for Homemade. Asymmetric one-sided-increase construction is a well-established technique with no single originating source.
heroPrompt: A wedge-shaped crochet shawl in deep plum DK yarn with horizontal ridged texture. Draped asymmetrically over one shoulder, the longer edge hanging down. Studio natural light.

glossaryTerms.definition: Working through only the back loop of a stitch top, leaving the front loop free. Creates a ridge on the right side of the fabric.
Two double crochets worked into the same stitch. Adds one stitch to the row count.

content.text: This shawl is a wedge shape measuring approximately 130cm along the long straight edge and 65cm at the widest point. It is worked from the narrow point outward in rows of double crochet worked into the back loop only. A single increase at one edge on every row creates the asymmetric angle: one edge of the shawl stays straight while the other curves outward, producing the characteristic wedge silhouette. Working into the back loop only leaves the front loops exposed as horizontal ridges across the fabric, giving a texture often described as garter-effect. DK weight on a 4mm hook produces firm, substantial fabric with good structure.

Yarn: approximately 450g of DK weight yarn. A smooth, tightly plied yarn makes the ridged texture clear. Hook: 4mm. You will also need a tapestry needle, scissors, and a tape measure. A stitch marker for the increase stitch is helpful. A foam blocking mat and rust-proof pins are useful for the final shaping.

18 dc and 20 rows to 10cm over dc worked into the back loop only, using a 4mm hook. This gauge is critical for the wedge to reach the correct dimensions. Work a 10cm swatch in dc-BLO and measure before starting the full piece.
dc-BLO: double crochet into back loop only
inc: 2 dc in the same stitch

The shawl starts at the point with a foundation chain of 3. The increase always happens at the end of the row (the widening edge). The ch 1 turning chain at the start of each row does not count as a stitch. Work all stitches into the back loop only unless stated otherwise.
Ch 1 (does not count as st), dc in 2nd ch from hook, dc in next ch, 2 dc in last ch (increase), turn. (4 sts)
Ch 1 (does not count as st), dc-BLO in each st to last st, 2 dc-BLO in last st (increase), turn. (5 sts)
Ch 1 (does not count as st), dc-BLO in each st to last st, 2 dc-BLO in last st (increase), turn.

Each row adds exactly 1 stitch. The row count equals the number of stitches in that row. Continue until the long (straight) edge measures approximately 130cm. At the stated gauge this is approximately 260 rows, ending with approximately 263 sts in the final row.
Work one row of dc through both loops evenly along the long straight edge for a neat finish. Do not increase at the corners; keep the edge flat.

Weave in all ends on the wrong side. Block by soaking in cool water and pressing out excess moisture. Pin the long straight edge to 130cm on a foam mat and ease the widest point to 65cm. Allow to dry completely. Blocking straightens the long edge and softens the fabric.
Hand wash in cool water with a gentle detergent. Reshape while damp and dry flat. Check the yarn label: wool-content yarns need cool water to avoid felting. Do not tumble dry.

The back-loop-only technique transfers well to scarves and cowls: a long dc-BLO rectangle in a finer yarn produces a stripy ribbed effect. For a triangle with increases on both sides and a more complex stitch pattern, try the ripple chevron shawl. If you want to explore the wedge shape in a lace yarn, the mohair lace shawl uses a similar one-edge-increase structure in lace weight.
